Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 33, verses 1–3:

Yā ayyuha al-Nabiyyu ittaqi Allāh ... wa kafā bi-Allāhi wakīlā (33:1–3)

This is the beginning of the surah in which the moral and social life of the new Islamic community is reorganized. This opening itself shows what the temperament of the Islamic system of life is, and what the rules and principles are on which the Islamic system practically rests. It shows what the concepts are through which it affects the conscience and morals of Muslims.

Islam is not merely guidance and admonition. Islam is not merely a name for a collection of moral teachings, nor is Islam merely a body of laws. Nor is it merely a name for customs and traditions. Islam is in fact a combination of all the things mentioned above. But even all these things together are not Islam. Islam is in fact a name for submitting one's head, surrendering to the will and the desire of Allah, bowing before the decree of Allah, and, above all, becoming ready to obey the commands and prohibitions of Allah: living one's life according to the system Allah has prescribed for mankind, without turning attention elsewhere, without turning towards any other direction, and without placing trust in any power other than Allah. The basic consciousness of Islam is that a person understands that he is subject to a law of nature which controls both himself and the whole universe spread around him. This system controls the spheres and the stars, and it controls all existence, whether hidden or manifest, unseen or present, whether people understand it or not, with the conviction that nothing is in their own control. They have only to follow the commands of Allah and to refrain from those things from which Allah has commanded them to refrain; to use the means and resources which Allah has provided for them, and then to await the results which Allah will bring about. This is the principle upon which all laws and all legal systems are founded, customs are founded, and manners and morals are founded; that is, the belief which exists in the conscience and consciousness should become practically manifest in human life, and there should be practical signs of it in a person's life, showing that the self has bowed before Allah and that he is living according to the Islamic system of life. The truth is that Shari'ah springs from Islam. A complete system of life is then built upon this Shari'ah, and these three matters are interrelated and integrated. This is Islam.

Accordingly, this surah begins with the enactment of new legislation for the Islamic society, namely, fear of Allah. The address is directed to the Nabi ﷺ, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the leader and organizer of this new society.

Yā ayyuha al-Nabiyyu ittaqi Allāh (33:1): "O Prophet, fear Allah." Fearing Allah means acknowledging that Allah is watching over us and that He is most exalted. This is the basic consciousness and the basic principle of Islam. Taqwa is the guardian within a person which inclines him to follow the commands of Allah. Therefore, it is through taqwa that the Islamic system of life is practically established. The second command is: do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Disregard their proposals and their guidance, do not seek their opinion, and do not accept their insistence.

Wa lā tuṭi' al-kāfirīna wa al-munāfiqīn (33:1): "Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." The command to obey the commands of Allah comes later here. It is mentioned even before that, that one should not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, because in that period there was great pressure from the disbelievers and the hypocrites upon the Muslims and upon the Messenger ﷺ. Therefore, here it is commanded that in the future practical organization of the Islamic society, too, one should not listen to their words and should not bow to their pressure. The Messenger ﷺ was commanded according to the circumstances of that time, but the Islamic movement should do the same in every time and place: wherever its own government is established, it should not accept the opinions and proposals of outsiders, so that the Islamic system of life may advance purely on its own policy and not be under the pressure of any outsider's policy.

No Muslim should be deceived into thinking that these disbelievers and hypocrites possess expertise and have knowledge and experience, as people today seek justifications for themselves in the age of their weakness, because Allah alone is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The system of life He has given to Muslims is founded upon knowledge and wisdom. There is no defect or fault in it, and people have no knowledge or wisdom in comparison with Allah. And immediately after this, the command is given:

Wa attabi' mā yūḥā ilayka min rabbika (33:2): "And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord." Because guidance for Muslims comes from Allah, not from the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Muslims follow God, not anyone else. In the very style of this verse there are some profound indications: follow what is being revealed (indicated) to you, specifically. Then this indication is from your Lord. It is as if special indications are being given here; understand them. And these indications are from Allah, the One who is obeyed.

Inna Allāha kāna bimā ta'malūna khabīrā (33:2): "Allah is aware of what you do." The guidance that Allah gives is based upon the highest level of knowledge and expertise. He is aware of the reality of your deeds. He is aware of your inclinations and your desires.

And the final guidance is:

Wa tawakkal 'alā Allāh wa kafā bi-Allāhi wakīlā (33:3): "Put your trust in Allah; Allah is sufficient as a Guardian." It is not important whether the disbelievers and hypocrites are with you or against you. Their cunning and conspiracies have no significance. Leave your affair to Allah; Allah will act within your affairs with His knowledge, His awareness, and His expertise. Leaving matters to Allah is what finally brings the heart to contentment and inner peace, and a person becomes aware of his own limits. He leaves matters beyond his limits to Allah, halts at his own bounds, and leaves what lies beyond to the one to whom it belongs. With complete tranquillity, full reliance, and full certainty, he performs his share of the work.

These three elements, the fear of Allah, the complete following of divine revelation, and reliance upon Allah alone, are the true provisions of any caller (dā'ī). Provided he remains detached from the disbelievers and hypocrites. These elements keep the Islamic call upon its path: fear of Allah, following the command that comes from Allah, and trust in Allah. These instructions are inscribed upon a powerful, profound observation, and this observation is based upon sensory experience.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 33, verse 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

Allah has not placed two hearts within a man's breast ﴿Allah has not placed two hearts within a man's body﴾. Every human being has one heart and one mind within him. Therefore his conception will also be one, and his system will also be one. He can walk only upon one straight path. Before him there will be one measure by which he weighs good and evil, and by one measure he will weigh events and values. If this does not happen, his life will be broken into pieces. He will be a hypocrite. There will be ups and downs in his life, and he will not be upon the straight path. It is not possible for a person to take his moral conduct and etiquette from one source, his constitution and law from another source, his social and economic system from a third source, and his arts and philosophies from a fourth source. Such mixed ideas cannot be gathered in one heart. Such a person and his personality will be fragmented, and his existence will not be able to endure.

A man of conviction, who truly possesses a doctrine and a belief, cannot be one who holds no doctrinal position in the smallest or greatest matter of life. He at every moment adopts values in accordance with the demands of his doctrines, and it is simply not possible that he should say a word, or make a movement, or form an intention or make a thought, and be unaffected by his doctrines or be detached from his faith. Because Allah has not placed two hearts in the chest of any human being. There is one heart, one belief, one action, one direction, and one measure and standard.

A man of conviction cannot say that he did this deed in his personal capacity and that he did that deed in his capacity as a Muslim, as today's politicians do, or as collective assemblies do, or as scholarly societies do. In short, man is one, his heart is one, his doctrine is one, his qibla is one, his conception is one, his standards of values and good and evil are one, and all of this is within his beliefs.

In short, with this one heart a person lives alone, lives within the family, lives within the community, lives within the government, lives in the world, lives in concealment and lives openly. He lives as a worker and as an employer, he lives as a ruler and as one ruled. He lives in difficulties and in ease. In short, this is his colour. It does not change. Neither does its standard change, nor does its value change. Nor does his thinking change.

﴿Allah has not placed two hearts within a man's body﴾ (33: 4). Therefore, the method of any doctrinal Islam is one, the path is one, the direction is one. It bows only before the command of Allah. If the heart is one, then the deity is also one, the master is also one, the way of life is also one, and if anyone is not like this, then his life will be scattered and he will be broken into pieces. After this decisive observation and after the determination of the way of life, the context now begins legal reforms. First, the law of zihar and the law of adoption (mutabanni) are abrogated, so that the family may be purified of external elements and built upon pure kinship and natural foundations.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers...﴾ to ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (4–5)

﴿...﴾

In the Jahiliyyah, the custom was that a man would say to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." That is, you are forbidden to me just as the mother is forbidden. From that very moment, intercourse with her would become forbidden to him. Now she would be left in suspension, neither a divorcee so that another could marry her, nor could she become his wife. And this was the greatest of the oppressions against women, and one of the mistreatments of the Jahiliyyah era.

Islam began its reforms first with the family system. It removed this oppression that occurred within the family. And the truth is that the family is the first circle of human association. Therefore Islam gave much attention to the family system so that the training ground in which children are raised would have a pleasant atmosphere and be peaceful. Thus the woman was relieved of this great burden and released from this state of captivity. And the relations between husband and wife were re-established upon justice and fairness. Thus this law was enacted.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ (33: 4). "He has not made your wives, whom you liken to your mothers through zihar, your mothers." For merely calling a wife "mother" with the tongue does not make her a mother. According to the reality of the matter, a mother is a mother and a wife is a wife. Merely by uttering a word, the nature of relationships and ties does not change. This is why an everlasting prohibition is not established by zihar, as the mother is forbidden in the way she was in the Jahiliyyah.

It is narrated in the reports that in Surah al-Mujadila the oppressive law of zihar was nullified, and the event was as follows: Aws ibn al-Samit did zihar with his wife Khawlah bint Tha'labah. She came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and made this claim: "O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he has consumed my wealth, he has destroyed my youth, my belly has swollen, my age has increased and my children have ended; and he has done zihar with me." The Prophet ﷺ said, "I think that you have become forbidden to him." She presented her complaint repeatedly. Upon this the following verses of Surah al-Mujadila were revealed:

﴿Indeed, Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. And Allah hears your exchange; indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing. Those among you who divorce their wives by zihar — their wives are not their mothers. Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them. And indeed, they say an unacceptable word and a lie. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving. And those who divorce their wives by zihar and then wish to retract what they said — then (the penance is) the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished thereby, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do. And whoever does not find (a slave) — then fasting for two months consecutively before they touch one another. And whoever is unable — then feeding sixty needy people. That is so that you believe in Allah and His Messenger. And these are the limits of Allah; and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ (58: 1–4).

Under this law, because of zihar, the husband and wife were temporarily separated from one another, and the everlasting prohibition that existed under the former law was abolished. And if the husband and wife wish to resume their marital life together, then before that they must free a slave, or fast for two consecutive months, or feed sixty needy people. Thus the wife becomes lawful to the husband again, and the marital life of both begins anew as before. And this new law is realistic and based on actual circumstances.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ (33: 4). "Allah has not made your wives, whom you liken to your mothers through zihar, your mothers." Because of this Jahiliyyah custom, the family would be ended forever, and on the other hand it was a permanent oppression upon the woman, and she would be left as if buried alive. Thus disturbance, chaos and complications would arise within family relations, and all of this was due to the man's personal desires and their supremacy and violence in Jahiliyyah society. This was the matter of zihar. The law of adoption (mutabanni), and calling people by names other than their fathers' names, was also a cause of concern for the family system, and due to it the harmony of a family was disturbed. Despite the fact that in Arab society chastity and lineage were greatly valued and lineage was a source of pride, alongside this pride certain weak aspects were also present in Arab society. Except for a few families, these weaknesses were generally present.

Among some people there were sons whose fathers were not known at all. When some people found such young men pleasing, they would take them as their sons, count them within their lineage, and the two would become heirs of one another.

Some sons had known fathers, but sometimes a person would find a certain boy pleasing and would take him as his son, and would make him a sharer in his lineage. Among the people he would become known as "the son of so-and-so." He would become a member of that family. This matter occurred especially with prisoners of war and abducted people. In wars and raids, children and young boys would be taken captive. Some people would take such people as their sons, give them their name, and he would become known by it, and he would perform the rights and duties of a son.

Among them was Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi. This is an Arab tribe; in the days of Jahiliyyah, in one of the raids, he was taken captive. Hakim ibn Hizam bought him for his paternal aunt Khadijah. When the Prophet ﷺ took Khadijah into his marriage, she gifted him to the Messenger ﷺ. After this, his father and his son demanded his release, and the Messenger ﷺ gave him the choice, and Zayd chose the Messenger ﷺ. The Messenger ﷺ freed him and made him his adopted son, and people began to call him Zayd ibn Muhammad. Among the slaves, he was the first to believe in the Messenger ﷺ.

When Islam began to establish family relations upon their natural and innate foundations, sought to strengthen family ties, and limited the family to its pure familial bounds, it abolished the Jahiliyyah law of adoption and established family relations on the basis of lineage, that is, blood ties based on the foundation of father and son. And it commanded this:

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ (33: 4).

﴿That is your saying by your mouths﴾ (33: 4). Mere words do not change facts and realities. And merely by words, blood ties are not established, nor do rights of inheritance arise. And by the tongue alone these relationships are not like those that exist when a living child is born from a living mother or is born from a true father.

﴿And Allah says the truth, and He guides to the [right] way﴾ (33: 4). He speaks the absolute truth, in which there is no falsehood, and among those truths is this: that family laws and relationships should be based upon reality, that is, upon the ties of blood and lineage, and not merely upon verbal statements. He takes the straight path in legislation and guides towards it. This is the natural law, and man-made laws cannot stand against these natural laws, especially when they are not realities but mere empty words, expressions with no meaning. Therefore real laws and relationships prevail over such laws and ties that are based on what is straight.

﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ (33: 5). "Call adopted sons by the names of their fathers. This is more just in the sight of Allah." The just matter is that a son should be called by his father's name. This is justice to the father from whose body this piece became separate and became a person. It is also justice to the son, and between these two there is justice in inheritance. Only father and son can be true helpers to one another. The son can be a trustee of the father's hidden qualities, and also a trustee of the characteristics of his ancestors. This is justice in the sense that every right is placed in its proper position, and relationships are established upon natural principles. Neither the father's right is violated nor the son's right is violated. The non-biological father will not have to bear the responsibilities of being a father, nor will he obtain the benefits to which he was not entitled. Neither will the adopter take on unnecessary responsibilities, nor will he be able to take benefits to which he was not entitled.

This is the familial system due to which balance arises in the responsibilities of the family, and the family is established upon very firm, deep and realistic foundations. Its foundation is truth, uprightness and harmony with nature. Any system which ignores the family system can never succeed. It rests upon weak, feeble and counterfeit foundations, and no such system can remain alive. Seeing that in the Jahiliyyah era there was great disorder in family relations, and likewise disorder in sexual relations, as a result of which lineages became greatly mixed, and sometimes people did not even know their fathers, Islam made provision in this matter, because Islam's intention was to reorganise the family system afresh. And Islam was striving to form a social order on the basis of the family. Therefore, for those whose ancestors were not known, it gave them a place within the Islamic community. This was the station of Islamic brotherhood.

﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your protégés﴾ (33: 5). The brotherhood in religion is a moral and spiritual bond, and no legal rights and duties were attached to it, such as the obligation of inheritance and its payment, whereas upon making someone an adopted son these legal rights and duties were established. This is so that these people too should have some place and connection within the Islamic community.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 33, verses 4–5 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if you do not know their fathers﴾ (33:5). From this it becomes clear that in the society of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah) there was great disorder with regard to lineage. As a consequence, there was also disorder in matters of sexual relations. To protect against this disorder, Islam reorganised the family system anew, and thus the family system was established on firm foundations.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 33, verse 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

Allah has not placed two hearts within a man's breast ﴿Allah has not placed two hearts within a man's body﴾. Every human being has one heart and one mind within him. Therefore his conception will also be one, and his system will also be one. He can walk only upon one straight path. Before him there will be one measure by which he weighs good and evil, and by one measure he will weigh events and values. If this does not happen, his life will be broken into pieces. He will be a hypocrite. There will be ups and downs in his life, and he will not be upon the straight path. It is not possible for a person to take his moral conduct and etiquette from one source, his constitution and law from another source, his social and economic system from a third source, and his arts and philosophies from a fourth source. Such mixed ideas cannot be gathered in one heart. Such a person and his personality will be fragmented, and his existence will not be able to endure.

A man of conviction, who truly possesses a doctrine and a belief, cannot be one who holds no doctrinal position in the smallest or greatest matter of life. He at every moment adopts values in accordance with the demands of his doctrines, and it is simply not possible that he should say a word, or make a movement, or form an intention or make a thought, and be unaffected by his doctrines or be detached from his faith. Because Allah has not placed two hearts in the chest of any human being. There is one heart, one belief, one action, one direction, and one measure and standard.

A man of conviction cannot say that he did this deed in his personal capacity and that he did that deed in his capacity as a Muslim, as today's politicians do, or as collective assemblies do, or as scholarly societies do. In short, man is one, his heart is one, his doctrine is one, his qibla is one, his conception is one, his standards of values and good and evil are one, and all of this is within his beliefs.

In short, with this one heart a person lives alone, lives within the family, lives within the community, lives within the government, lives in the world, lives in concealment and lives openly. He lives as a worker and as an employer, he lives as a ruler and as one ruled. He lives in difficulties and in ease. In short, this is his colour. It does not change. Neither does its standard change, nor does its value change. Nor does his thinking change.

﴿Allah has not placed two hearts within a man's body﴾ (33: 4). Therefore, the method of any doctrinal Islam is one, the path is one, the direction is one. It bows only before the command of Allah. If the heart is one, then the deity is also one, the master is also one, the way of life is also one, and if anyone is not like this, then his life will be scattered and he will be broken into pieces. After this decisive observation and after the determination of the way of life, the context now begins legal reforms. First, the law of zihar and the law of adoption (mutabanni) are abrogated, so that the family may be purified of external elements and built upon pure kinship and natural foundations.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers...﴾ to ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (4–5)

﴿...﴾

In the Jahiliyyah, the custom was that a man would say to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." That is, you are forbidden to me just as the mother is forbidden. From that very moment, intercourse with her would become forbidden to him. Now she would be left in suspension, neither a divorcee so that another could marry her, nor could she become his wife. And this was the greatest of the oppressions against women, and one of the mistreatments of the Jahiliyyah era.

Islam began its reforms first with the family system. It removed this oppression that occurred within the family. And the truth is that the family is the first circle of human association. Therefore Islam gave much attention to the family system so that the training ground in which children are raised would have a pleasant atmosphere and be peaceful. Thus the woman was relieved of this great burden and released from this state of captivity. And the relations between husband and wife were re-established upon justice and fairness. Thus this law was enacted.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ (33: 4). "He has not made your wives, whom you liken to your mothers through zihar, your mothers." For merely calling a wife "mother" with the tongue does not make her a mother. According to the reality of the matter, a mother is a mother and a wife is a wife. Merely by uttering a word, the nature of relationships and ties does not change. This is why an everlasting prohibition is not established by zihar, as the mother is forbidden in the way she was in the Jahiliyyah.

It is narrated in the reports that in Surah al-Mujadila the oppressive law of zihar was nullified, and the event was as follows: Aws ibn al-Samit did zihar with his wife Khawlah bint Tha'labah. She came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and made this claim: "O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he has consumed my wealth, he has destroyed my youth, my belly has swollen, my age has increased and my children have ended; and he has done zihar with me." The Prophet ﷺ said, "I think that you have become forbidden to him." She presented her complaint repeatedly. Upon this the following verses of Surah al-Mujadila were revealed:

﴿Indeed, Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. And Allah hears your exchange; indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing. Those among you who divorce their wives by zihar — their wives are not their mothers. Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them. And indeed, they say an unacceptable word and a lie. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving. And those who divorce their wives by zihar and then wish to retract what they said — then (the penance is) the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished thereby, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do. And whoever does not find (a slave) — then fasting for two months consecutively before they touch one another. And whoever is unable — then feeding sixty needy people. That is so that you believe in Allah and His Messenger. And these are the limits of Allah; and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ (58: 1–4).

Under this law, because of zihar, the husband and wife were temporarily separated from one another, and the everlasting prohibition that existed under the former law was abolished. And if the husband and wife wish to resume their marital life together, then before that they must free a slave, or fast for two consecutive months, or feed sixty needy people. Thus the wife becomes lawful to the husband again, and the marital life of both begins anew as before. And this new law is realistic and based on actual circumstances.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ (33: 4). "Allah has not made your wives, whom you liken to your mothers through zihar, your mothers." Because of this Jahiliyyah custom, the family would be ended forever, and on the other hand it was a permanent oppression upon the woman, and she would be left as if buried alive. Thus disturbance, chaos and complications would arise within family relations, and all of this was due to the man's personal desires and their supremacy and violence in Jahiliyyah society. This was the matter of zihar. The law of adoption (mutabanni), and calling people by names other than their fathers' names, was also a cause of concern for the family system, and due to it the harmony of a family was disturbed. Despite the fact that in Arab society chastity and lineage were greatly valued and lineage was a source of pride, alongside this pride certain weak aspects were also present in Arab society. Except for a few families, these weaknesses were generally present.

Among some people there were sons whose fathers were not known at all. When some people found such young men pleasing, they would take them as their sons, count them within their lineage, and the two would become heirs of one another.

Some sons had known fathers, but sometimes a person would find a certain boy pleasing and would take him as his son, and would make him a sharer in his lineage. Among the people he would become known as "the son of so-and-so." He would become a member of that family. This matter occurred especially with prisoners of war and abducted people. In wars and raids, children and young boys would be taken captive. Some people would take such people as their sons, give them their name, and he would become known by it, and he would perform the rights and duties of a son.

Among them was Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi. This is an Arab tribe; in the days of Jahiliyyah, in one of the raids, he was taken captive. Hakim ibn Hizam bought him for his paternal aunt Khadijah. When the Prophet ﷺ took Khadijah into his marriage, she gifted him to the Messenger ﷺ. After this, his father and his son demanded his release, and the Messenger ﷺ gave him the choice, and Zayd chose the Messenger ﷺ. The Messenger ﷺ freed him and made him his adopted son, and people began to call him Zayd ibn Muhammad. Among the slaves, he was the first to believe in the Messenger ﷺ.

When Islam began to establish family relations upon their natural and innate foundations, sought to strengthen family ties, and limited the family to its pure familial bounds, it abolished the Jahiliyyah law of adoption and established family relations on the basis of lineage, that is, blood ties based on the foundation of father and son. And it commanded this:

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ (33: 4).

﴿That is your saying by your mouths﴾ (33: 4). Mere words do not change facts and realities. And merely by words, blood ties are not established, nor do rights of inheritance arise. And by the tongue alone these relationships are not like those that exist when a living child is born from a living mother or is born from a true father.

﴿And Allah says the truth, and He guides to the [right] way﴾ (33: 4). He speaks the absolute truth, in which there is no falsehood, and among those truths is this: that family laws and relationships should be based upon reality, that is, upon the ties of blood and lineage, and not merely upon verbal statements. He takes the straight path in legislation and guides towards it. This is the natural law, and man-made laws cannot stand against these natural laws, especially when they are not realities but mere empty words, expressions with no meaning. Therefore real laws and relationships prevail over such laws and ties that are based on what is straight.

﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ (33: 5). "Call adopted sons by the names of their fathers. This is more just in the sight of Allah." The just matter is that a son should be called by his father's name. This is justice to the father from whose body this piece became separate and became a person. It is also justice to the son, and between these two there is justice in inheritance. Only father and son can be true helpers to one another. The son can be a trustee of the father's hidden qualities, and also a trustee of the characteristics of his ancestors. This is justice in the sense that every right is placed in its proper position, and relationships are established upon natural principles. Neither the father's right is violated nor the son's right is violated. The non-biological father will not have to bear the responsibilities of being a father, nor will he obtain the benefits to which he was not entitled. Neither will the adopter take on unnecessary responsibilities, nor will he be able to take benefits to which he was not entitled.

This is the familial system due to which balance arises in the responsibilities of the family, and the family is established upon very firm, deep and realistic foundations. Its foundation is truth, uprightness and harmony with nature. Any system which ignores the family system can never succeed. It rests upon weak, feeble and counterfeit foundations, and no such system can remain alive. Seeing that in the Jahiliyyah era there was great disorder in family relations, and likewise disorder in sexual relations, as a result of which lineages became greatly mixed, and sometimes people did not even know their fathers, Islam made provision in this matter, because Islam's intention was to reorganise the family system afresh. And Islam was striving to form a social order on the basis of the family. Therefore, for those whose ancestors were not known, it gave them a place within the Islamic community. This was the station of Islamic brotherhood.

﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your protégés﴾ (33: 5). The brotherhood in religion is a moral and spiritual bond, and no legal rights and duties were attached to it, such as the obligation of inheritance and its payment, whereas upon making someone an adopted son these legal rights and duties were established. This is so that these people too should have some place and connection within the Islamic community.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 33, verses 4–5 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if you do not know their fathers﴾ (33:5). From this it becomes clear that in the society of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah) there was great disorder with regard to lineage. As a consequence, there was also disorder in matters of sexual relations. To protect against this disorder, Islam reorganised the family system anew, and thus the family system was established on firm foundations.

Having returned lineages to their true reality, it is now said that if a person does not know his true lineage and, in the matter of lineage, says something mistaken, there is no fault upon him.

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in, but [what matters is] what your hearts intend﴾ (33:5). There is no blame for what you say unintentionally, but there is blame for what your hearts resolve upon. This is a great mercy of Allah, that Allah does not impose upon anyone a command that they have no capacity to fulfil.

﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (33:5). The Prophet (ﷺ) gave great emphasis and severity regarding lineage, because the aim of Islam was that the new society be organised along lines in which there would be no disorder, just as in jahili societies no one knows for certain whose child another is. For this reason, those who conceal their lineage were given a severe warning, and the charge of kufr was applied to them. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim, from Ibn 'Ulayyah, from 'Uyaynah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said that Allah said:

﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers. That is more just in the sight of Allah. But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your associates﴾ (33:5). My father said, "'Uyaynah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman says": "By Allah, I am certain that if someone knew that his father was a donkey, he would still attribute himself to him."

And a hadith states:

"Whoever claims to be [the son] of other than his father, while knowing it is not so, has committed kufr (disbelief)."

This warning is in accordance with the policy by which Islam seeks to keep the family and family ties free from every doubt and suspicion, and Islam wishes to keep the line of lineage sound, intact and of established authenticity, so that the Islamic society may be built upon it, and that this society may be a correct and pure society.

After this, another interim law is amended. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, he established brotherhood (mu'akhah) between the Ansar and the Muhajirun. Before Islam, in the Age of Ignorance, there was no such system. This system was devised by Islam after the Hijrah, because the Muhajirun had left their wealth behind in Makkah; they arrived here empty-handed. Likewise, in Madinah too there were people whom their families had expelled from their homes because they had become Muslims. After the abolition of the brotherhood, the Prophet (ﷺ) was given general guardianship (wilayah 'ammah), and this guardianship was declared to take precedence over all other forms of guardianship. Along with the Prophet (ﷺ) becoming the general guardian, his wives were also declared the spiritual mothers (of the believers).

The Muhajirun migrated from Makkah to Madinah. They left everything behind and came to Madinah, fleeing to Allah and taking only their faith with them. They gave precedence to their creed over the ties of their clan, their stores of wealth, their means of livelihood, the memories of their childhood, and their circles of companions and friends. These people left with nothing but their faith and abandoned everything else. By migrating in this manner, they gave up everything that is dear to every human being: their families, their sons and daughters, and their other relatives. This was a living example, and it occurred on this earth: people abandoned everything for the sake of their beliefs alone. Their hearts were overwhelmed by their creed, so that no other thing remained in their hearts apart from this creed and ideology. Their personalities became unified.

﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ (33:4). In the same way, a new situation arose in Madinah. Some members of certain families entered Islam, while others continued to commit shirk. Relations between them were severed. In short, a tremor shook the family ties, and the social order was also thrown into disarray. It was also a reality that the Islamic society was newly born, and the Islamic state was not yet firmly established. In fact, it was still a proposed system, most of which existed only in concepts. Its stable institutions had not yet been formed.

In short, an ideological storm arose in Madinah. It was the storm of the Islamic worldview. It swept away all sentiments, all customs and traditions, and all ties and relationships, and within this new society only the Islamic bond remained. All hearts were united upon the Islamic creed. Family, lineage, tribe, friendship, and national ties were buried beneath the waves of this ideology, and these new units, which had already become integrated within Islamic society, merged with one another. A new society came into being, and people gathered on the basis of Islamic brotherhood. These people were not bound together by Islamic brotherhood through any law or command; rather, the Islamic worldview had created within them a tremendous sense of unity. This consciousness was so firm that there was no precedent for it in human history. In short, in this way a very large family came into being, a community was formed. A family of this kind could not be established on the basis of a government, nor could social conditions produce it. In any case, this brotherhood was Islamic; it was an inner consciousness.

The Muhajirun arrived and settled among the Ansar brothers, who handled the Muhajirun's affairs in Madinah in an excellent manner. They welcomed them, admitted them into their hearts and homes, and honored them greatly. They shared their wealth with them and vied with one another in giving them refuge. There was such competition that a Muhajir could only be accommodated in an Ansari's home by drawing lots, because the Muhajirun were few and the Ansar, who wished to offer shelter, were many. This refuge was given with complete trust and enthusiasm. It was given with genuine joy and heartfelt delight. This refuge was free of every kind of natural stinginess, arrogance, and display.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) established brotherhood (muwakhat, the bond of brotherhood) between the Muhajirun and the Ansar. This system was unparalleled in the history of ideological societies. This brotherhood effectively took the place of blood kinship. Accordingly, under this system, people inherited from one another and also fulfilled the other obligations and duties of collective mutual support (takaful), such as diyah (blood money) and so on.

This consciousness of unity reached a very high level, and the Muslims solemnly strengthened these bonds. In this way they became brothers, just as they had accepted the other commands of Islam. Thus this society took the form of a stable government, and the principles of brotherhood took on the character of an official governmental institution, a legal system, and a permanent state of affairs. Indeed, its roots became very deep. It was also necessary to protect this new community and society from any shock. This system, which was taking on a permanent form, was, according to Allah's will, a temporary arrangement.

Any community that faces circumstances like those of the Islamic community of Madinah needs to develop this kind of consciousness, so that under its influence a permanent society and government may come into being: a legal system and Muslim institutions, so that the problems confronting such a community in extraordinary circumstances can be solved, and in this way communal life may be advanced. This work should continue until conditions return to normal.

Although Islam wishes to keep this kind of consciousness alive at all times, and wishes that fountains of this kind of brotherhood and self-sacrifice continually gush forth within Islamic society, and that springs of proof and strength keep flowing from them, Islam also wishes that the development of society should accord with natural conditions, and that the system of collective life should not rest merely on temporary emotions and temporary upheavals, which are used in extraordinary circumstances. Rather, society should be built upon natural and normal conditions, and the system should continue to function according to the norm, until unnecessary and exceptional circumstances come to an end.

After the Battle of Badr, when conditions in Madinah had somewhat returned to normal, the Islamic state became firmly established, social conditions became stable in accordance with the norm, and arrangements for employment were made for the people. The small raids that the Islamic armies had begun to undertake, and the Battle of Badr that followed, improved the financial circumstances of the people. Especially after the expulsion of the Banu Qaynuqa, the Muslims gathered considerable wealth. As soon as arrangements for social security were established within society through other means, the Qur'an did not hesitate for a single moment in abrogating this extraordinary system of brotherhood, and the system of collective support was linked to the system of family and lineage. However, Islam kept intact the consciousness and feeling behind Islamic brotherhood and muwakhat, so that if such extraordinary circumstances arose again, this system could be re-established. In this way the system of collective support within the Muslim community was returned to its true condition: mutual support in inheritance and blood money was returned to blood and lineage, just as it had already been written in the Book of Allah.

﴿But those related by blood are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah than the [other] believers and the emigrants, except that you do to your allies a kindness﴾ (33:6). ﴿This is written in the Book﴾ (33:6). It was decided that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the general guardian (wali), and this is a guardianship that takes precedence over kinship, and even over the believers' own selves.

﴿The Prophet is more entitled to the believers than themselves﴾ (33:6). It was also decided that the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) are spiritual mothers.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾ (33:6). The guardianship of the Prophet (ﷺ) is a general guardianship; he had the authority to give the Muslim community a complete system of life. The believers were commanded to send blessings and greetings upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and there is no path for them except to adopt the matters that the Prophet (ﷺ) has chosen for them.

﴿None of you [truly] believes until his desires are subservient to that which I have brought﴾. This includes the consciousness of the Muslims. Therefore, the person of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) must be more beloved to them than all other things. They cannot love anyone, even themselves, more than the Messenger. No person or thing should take precedence over the person of the Messenger in their hearts. In the authentic hadith it is stated:

"By the One in whose hand is my soul, none of you truly believes until I become more beloved to him than his own self, his wealth, his children, and all of mankind."

In an authentic hadith, Hazrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than everything except my own self.' Upon this the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'No, O Umar, until I become dearer to you than your own self.' Then he said, 'Now, O Umar.'" This was not merely words. It was a lofty standard which the Islamic society had reached, and no heart can attain it unless it receives a touch from the higher realm, and raises its gaze to the lofty horizon. This is the station where the attraction of one's self and its profound love also become directed toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A person has an unimaginable love for himself and for what belongs to him. Sometimes he feels that he has gained control over his feelings and sentiments, has tamed his own soul, and has come down from the heights of self-love. But when his self and his interests are touched, he leaps up as if a snake has bitten him. He feels that sting in such a way that he cannot bear it at all. Even if he bears it, this pain settles into his consciousness and takes root in its depths. Sometimes a person is ready to sacrifice his entire life, but he cannot bear personal humiliation. Nor can he bear any defect that is attributed to his person and qualities, even if someone outwardly shows that they do not object to such things or do not care about them. In short, to master oneself, and to give greater importance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and one's ideology even above one's own self, is not merely a verbal matter that anyone can easily declare. It is a lofty station which no one can reach without a touch from the higher realm. It requires long struggle, long discipline, constant vigilance, and a sincere desire, accompanied by the special help of Allah. This is the great struggle (jihad), which has been called the greater jihad of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is a station to which even a personality like Hazrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) needed a warning and correction from the Prophet (ﷺ). That was a spark from his pure heart, as a result of which Hazrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) reached that lofty station in an instant.

In the general guardianship, too, certain obligations fall upon the members of the Ummah in relation to the Prophet (ﷺ). In an authentic hadith it is stated: "I am more beloved to every believer than all people, in this world and in the Hereafter. If you wish, recite this verse: ﴿The Prophet is more entitled to the believers than themselves﴾ (33:6). Therefore, whichever believer leaves behind wealth, it will go to his asabah (male agnatic relatives), whoever they may be. And if he has debts or is a minor (dependent), let him come to me, for I am his guardian."

The meaning is that if a believer dies and his estate contains no wealth with which his debts can be repaid, then I will pay his debts, and if he has dependents, I will look after them, if they are young children. Apart from this, under ordinary circumstances, the lives of ordinary people will proceed according to natural conditions and in accordance with their own efforts. There is no need for the extraordinary enthusiasm that a people displays in extraordinary circumstances. Although the system of brotherhood was abolished in a legal sense, it remained in the moral sphere. Therefore, if a friend makes a bequest for his friend, he is permitted to bequeath up to one-third of his property (thuluth).

﴿Except that you do to your allies a kindness﴾ (33:6). All these measures are firmly linked to this principle, and it is explained that this is the will and decree of Allah, and ﴿that was written in the Book﴾ (33:6). Therefore, let hearts be at ease, and hold firmly to the principle to which all laws return. In this way, the economic life of people is now established upon its natural principles, and it proceeds with great seriousness and tranquility. It has not been placed upon a standard that can only be established in extraordinary circumstances, within limited communities and limited individuals.

However, Islam does not close this generous source, so that if in the future the Islamic community should need it in some exceptional situation, it may put this spirit into action, that is, in emergency circumstances. This is in harmony with the fact that all of this was already written in the Book, and the will of Allah had determined that it would remain an eternal law and a continuous method. In this context, reference is made to the covenant made with the Prophets, especially with the Ulul-Azm (steadfast) Prophets, that they accept the responsibility of establishing the Islamic system and remain steadfast in this movement, continuing the work of preaching and mobilization among the people, and continuing this call among the nations to which they were sent. This is so that the message may serve as proof against the people, that the message had reached them, and that they are responsible for their misguidance and their guidance, for disbelief and faith. For after the preaching of the Prophets, the proof is indeed complete.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 33, verses 7–8:

﴿And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you [O Muhammad], and from Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, son of Mary. And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ (33:7–8)... This covenant was taken continuously from Noah (peace be upon him) down to Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It is the one covenant-bearing system and the one trust. Every prophet received it from his predecessor and handed it on to the one who came after him.

At the outset, it was mentioned concerning all the prophets that We took a covenant from them, and afterwards it was specifically mentioned concerning the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ) with the words "and from you" (wa minka), because you are the Seal of the Prophets and your call is universal. After that, the names of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulul-azm) were enumerated: Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them). Following the mention of the people of the covenant, it is now explained what that covenant was and what kind it was: it was a very firm covenant, a very weighty covenant.

﴿A solemn covenant﴾ (33:7). This points to the literal meaning of the word *mithaq*. In the lexicon, *mithaq* refers to a twisted rope. Metaphorically, it is used for a covenant. The use of this word is intended to give concrete form to an abstract meaning, so that human consciousness may well understand that this was a firm and important covenant, taken from such great prophets that they should receive revelation, convey it, establish the Islamic system in accordance with it, and bear its responsibilities with the utmost trustworthiness and steadfastness.

﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ (33:8). "So that Allah may ask the truthful people about their truthfulness." The truthful (*al-sadiqun*) are the believers, because they spoke the truth and accepted the true faith. All other people apart from them are liars, because their beliefs are false and their words are false. Therefore the expression has a special meaning. The question to the truthful will be like that which a capable student is asked by his teacher before people in a gathering or ceremony: how many marks did you get, how did you answer, and thus you achieved success. This question will be asked openly before all people to honour them, so that all who hear will also praise them. Likewise, on the Day of Resurrection, Allah will ask the truthful in order to honour them.

Now, as for the others who adopted false ideas and uttered lies, although before them was presented the greatest matter of this universe, in which they had to say either the true word or a false one, they will be questioned, and a punishment will be present for them, and it will stand ready.

﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ (33:8).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 33, verses 7–8:
